newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Investors seen cool to S.Korea foreign share limit.
newsitem.headline: Investors seen cool to S.Korea foreign share limit.

text.p: The foreign shareholding limit in South Korean companies will rise three percentage points from Friday, but analysts warned a rash of corporate failures and a slumping economy had cooled interest in all but blue chips.
"A lot of people have been burned," said Stephen Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Investment and Securities.

"It's one thing if a company's earnings or profits are way down or off. That puts a fund manager's bonus at risk. It's another thing to invest in a company that goes bankrupt. That could cost him his job."

The ceiling on foreign-owned shares, which is applied to individual companies, will increase to 23 percent from 20 percent. It was raised twice in 1996 and a further increase of three percentage points is expected later this year.
Two corporate bankruptcies this year, Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March, have underscored the precarious position of many South Korean companies.

The 19th-ranked Jinro Group, whose flagship is the country's largest and oldest distilled spirits maker, avoided becoming the year's third high-profile collapse only after banks promised to defer its debt payments and extend fresh loans.
"It has spooked a lot of foreign investors, particularly first-time investors who were really gung ho about Korea," said Edward Bang, Korea strategist for HSBC James Capel in Hong Kong.

"I really think foreigners are fed up. They have more of a show-me attitude," Bang said. Foreign investors had not forgotten that net earnings of South Korean companies dropped 64.5 percent on average last year, he added.

Analysts said they believe the Korean economy, sideswiped by slumping exports of key products such as computer chips and the weak Japanese yen, would bottom out in the fourth quarter. But they said sceptical foreign investors wanted proof.

"The crux of our problem is most Korean brokers and most foreign brokers have tended to suggest in the recent two years that things were going to get better and by and large they have not," said Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K.) Ltd, a securities firm.

Ssangyong's Marvin said: "We have no clear, palpable evidence of the bottom yet. If in the second half of the year we get a bottoming and leading indicators point to recovery, there will be a little more enthusiasm for Korean equities."

Still, there was widespread agreement that newly available shares in prized companies such as Pohang Iron and Steel Co (POSCO), Samsung Electronics Co and SK Telecom Co would be snapped up almost immediately, analysts said.
In the case of POSCO, the new limit will make another 2.6 million shares newly available to foreign investors.

"The fact of the matter is, what happened to Hanbo and Jinro will not happen to companies like SK Telecom or POSCO," said Del Ricks, head of research at Barclays de Zoete Wedd in Seoul. "There is a lot of interest in the core blue chips."

The consensus among Korean brokers is that 500 billion to one trillion won ($560 million to $1.12 billion) in foreign funds will flow into the market as a result of the foreign shareholding limit increase.
Foreign brokers said they expected foreign buying to be at the lower end of that estimate.
"For blue-chip stocks that trade at a premium, money will come in quickly," Ricks said.
